title: change two gas variables at once (T in kelvin, V) and combine the ratios
stem: A gas in a cylinder with a movable piston is at 1.0 atm, 300 K and 4.0 L. It is heated to 600 K while the piston is moved so that the volume becomes 8.0 L. No gas enters or leaves. What is the final pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 4.0 atm
choices.rationale: 4.0 atm treats the doubled volume as if it also raised the pressure, so both factors of 2 are multiplied together.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2.0 atm
choices.rationale: 2.0 atm accounts for the temperature increase only and ignores the larger volume, which lowers the pressure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 0.25 atm
choices.rationale: 0.25 atm inverts the temperature relation as well, as if a hotter gas had a lower pressure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1.0 atm
choices.rationale: Correct: P₂ = P₁ × (T₂/T₁) × (V₁/V₂) = 1.0 × 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 atm; the doubling of temperature is cancelled by the doubling of volume.

title: change two gas variables at once (T in kelvin, V) and combine the ratios (variant 1)
stem: A gas at 2.0 atm and 27°C occupies 3.0 L in a cylinder with a movable piston. It is heated to 177°C and the piston is pushed in until the volume is 2.4 L. No gas leaves. What is the final pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2.5 atm
choices.rationale: 2.5 atm accounts for the volume compression only and ignores that the gas was heated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3.0 atm
choices.rationale: 3.0 atm accounts for the temperature increase only and ignores the compression.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 3.75 atm

choices.label: D
choices.text: 16 atm
choices.rationale: 16 atm uses the Celsius temperatures 177 and 27 instead of kelvin, which overstates the temperature ratio.

title: change two gas variables at once (T in kelvin, V) and combine the ratios (variant 2)
stem: A 12.0 L sample of gas at 1.50 atm and 27°C is compressed to 4.0 L while it is cooled to -73°C. No gas leaves. What is the final pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 3.0 atm

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1.0 atm
choices.rationale: 1.0 atm uses only the temperature ratio and forgets that the volume fell to one third.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 4.5 atm
choices.rationale: 4.5 atm uses only the volume ratio and forgets that cooling lowers the pressure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0.75 atm
choices.rationale: 0.75 atm inverts the volume ratio and the temperature ratio, so the pressure falls when the gas is compressed.

title: change two gas variables at once (T in kelvin, V) and combine the ratios (variant 3)
stem: A gas at 3.0 atm, 400 K and 6.0 L is allowed to expand to 9.0 L while its temperature is lowered to 300 K. No gas enters or leaves. What is the final pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2.25 atm
choices.rationale: 2.25 atm accounts for the cooling only and ignores the expansion, which also lowers the pressure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2.0 atm
choices.rationale: 2.0 atm accounts for the expansion only and ignores the cooling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 3.4 atm
choices.rationale: 3.4 atm applies the volume ratio upside down (9.0/6.0), so it says the pressure rises when the gas expands.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1.5 atm

title: partial pressure in a mixture from moles, not mass
stem: A rigid 10.0 L vessel at 300 K holds 4.0 g of H₂ (2.0 g/mol) and 32.0 g of O₂ (32.0 g/mol). Use R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K). What is the partial pressure of O₂?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 2.46 atm
choices.rationale: Correct: n(O₂) = 32.0/32.0 = 1.00 mol; P = nRT/V = 1.00 × 0.0821 × 300 / 10.0 = 2.46 atm. (n(H₂) = 2.0 mol, total pressure 7.39 atm.).

choices.label: B
choices.text: 6.57 atm
choices.rationale: 6.57 atm uses the mass fraction of O₂ (32/36) of the total pressure, but pressure fractions follow mole fractions, and H₂ has twice as many moles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 7.39 atm
choices.rationale: 7.39 atm is the total pressure of both gases, not the share due to O₂.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 3.69 atm
choices.rationale: 3.69 atm assumes the two gases split the pressure equally, which would need equal numbers of moles.

title: partial pressure in a mixture from moles, not mass (variant 1)
stem: A rigid 5.00 L tank at 350 K holds 8.0 g of He (4.0 g/mol) and 28.0 g of N₂ (28.0 g/mol). Use R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K). What is the partial pressure of N₂?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 5.75 atm
choices.rationale: Correct: n(He) = 2.0 mol and n(N₂) = 1.0 mol; P(N₂) = 1.0 × 0.0821 × 350 / 5.00 = 5.75 atm (total 17.2 atm).

choices.label: B
choices.text: 17.2 atm
choices.rationale: 17.2 atm is the total pressure of the mixture, not the part due to N₂.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 13.4 atm
choices.rationale: 13.4 atm uses the mass fraction of N₂ (28/36), but N₂ is only one third of the moles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 8.62 atm
choices.rationale: 8.62 atm splits the total pressure equally between the two gases.

title: partial pressure in a mixture from moles, not mass (variant 2)
stem: A rigid vessel at 300 K holds 2.0 g of H₂ (2.0 g/mol) and 16.0 g of CH₄ (16.0 g/mol). Which comparison of the partial pressures is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CH₄ has a partial pressure 8 times that of H₂, because its mass is 8 times as large.
choices.rationale: Pressure follows the number of moles, not the mass, and the mass ratio of 8 is cancelled by the molar mass ratio of 8.

choices.label: B
choices.text: H₂ has the greater partial pressure, because its molecules are faster.
choices.rationale: H₂ molecules are faster, but they are also lighter, so each collision transfers less momentum, and the effects cancel at equal moles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The partial pressures are essentially equal, because each gas is present at about 1 mol.
choices.rationale: Correct: n(H₂) = 2.0/2.0 = 1.0 mol and n(CH₄) = 16.0/16.0 = 1.0 mol; same T and V, so equal partial pressures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: H₂ has the greater partial pressure, because lighter molecules take up less space.
choices.rationale: In an ideal gas the molecular size is ignored, so the size of the molecules does not set the partial pressure.

title: partial pressure in a mixture from moles, not mass (variant 3)
stem: A rigid container holds 7.0 g of N₂ (28 g/mol) and 4.0 g of He (4.0 g/mol). The total pressure is 3.00 atm. What is the partial pressure of He?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1.09 atm
choices.rationale: 1.09 atm uses the mass fraction of He (4/11) as the pressure fraction, instead of the mole fraction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1.50 atm
choices.rationale: 1.50 atm splits the total pressure equally between the two gases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 0.60 atm
choices.rationale: 0.60 atm is the partial pressure of N₂, the other gas, so the wrong gas was chosen.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 2.40 atm

title: read speed distributions as fractions of molecules
stem: A sample of N₂(g) at 300 K has 10% of its molecules moving faster than 700 m/s. The sample is heated to 450 K in a rigid container. Which statement about the heated sample is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: More than 10% of the molecules move faster than 700 m/s, and some molecules still move more slowly than the average speed at 300 K.
choices.rationale: Correct: raising T shifts the whole distribution to higher speeds, so the fraction above a fixed speed grows; the distribution still has a low-speed tail, so some molecules are slower than the old average.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fewer than 10% of the molecules move faster than 700 m/s, because the distribution becomes broader and flatter.
choices.rationale: A broader and flatter curve still has more area at high speeds, so the fraction above 700 m/s grows with temperature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exactly 10% of the molecules move faster than 700 m/s, because that fraction depends only on the gas, not on temperature.
choices.rationale: The fraction above a fixed speed depends strongly on temperature, because only the average kinetic energy scales simply.

choices.label: D
choices.text: More than 10% of the molecules move faster than 700 m/s, and no molecule moves more slowly than the average speed at 300 K.
choices.rationale: Temperature raises the average, but the distribution always keeps a tail of slow molecules, so a few molecules are still slower than the old average.

title: read speed distributions as fractions of molecules (variant 1)
stem: At 200 K, 15% of the Ar atoms in a sample move more slowly than 150 m/s. The sample is heated to 400 K in a rigid container. Which statement about the heated sample is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fewer than 15% move more slowly than 150 m/s, and the average speed doubles.
choices.rationale: Average speed is proportional to the square root of T, so doubling T raises the speed by about 1.41, not 2.

choices.label: B
choices.text: More than 15% move more slowly than 150 m/s, because collisions slow some atoms down.
choices.rationale: More collisions at higher temperature exchange energy but do not change the overall trend, and the average speed rises, so the slow fraction falls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fewer than 15% move more slowly than 150 m/s, and the average kinetic energy doubles.
choices.rationale: Correct: heating shifts the distribution upward, so the fraction below a fixed low speed falls; average kinetic energy is proportional to T, so it doubles, while the average speed rises only by a factor of √2.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exactly 15% move more slowly than 150 m/s, and the average kinetic energy doubles.
choices.rationale: The slow fraction cannot stay fixed while the whole distribution moves to higher speed.

title: read speed distributions as fractions of molecules (variant 2)
stem: He(g) and Ne(g) are in separate containers at the same temperature, 300 K. Which statement correctly compares their speeds?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every He atom moves faster than every Ne atom, because He atoms are lighter.
choices.rationale: The distributions overlap, so the fastest Ne atoms move faster than the slowest He atoms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A larger fraction of He atoms than Ne atoms moves faster than any chosen high speed, although the distributions overlap so some Ne atoms are faster than some He atoms.
choices.rationale: Correct: equal T gives equal average KE; He is lighter so its distribution is shifted to higher speeds, but both are broad curves that overlap.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fraction of atoms above any given speed is the same for both gases, because the average kinetic energies are equal.
choices.rationale: Equal average kinetic energy does not give equal speeds, because lighter atoms need a higher speed to have the same energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A larger fraction of Ne atoms than He atoms moves faster than any chosen speed, because Ne atoms have more momentum.
choices.rationale: Momentum differences do not raise speeds; at equal energy the heavier atoms move more slowly.

title: read speed distributions as fractions of molecules (variant 3)
stem: The speed distribution of CO₂(g) at 300 K is compared with that of the same sample of CO₂(g) at 600 K. Which description of the 600 K curve, relative to the 300 K curve, is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The peak is higher and narrower, because the molecules are more energetic and more alike.
choices.rationale: A wider range of speeds means a lower, broader curve, not a narrower one.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The peak is at the same speed but taller, because more molecules reach that speed.
choices.rationale: The most probable speed rises with temperature, so the peak moves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The peak is at a higher speed with the same height, and the area is larger because the molecules are more energetic.
choices.rationale: The area under the curve represents the total number of molecules, which does not change when the gas is heated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The peak is lower, broader and at a higher speed, and the area under the curve is the same.
choices.rationale: Correct: heating moves the most probable speed up, spreads the speeds over a wider range, so the peak lowers; the number of molecules, and so the area, is unchanged.

title: separate collision frequency, momentum per collision and speed in pressure
stem: Two rigid 2.0 L flasks at 300 K each hold 1.0 mol of gas. One holds He and the other holds Ar. Their pressures are equal. Which statement best explains this using kinetic molecular theory?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The He atoms are faster, so they hit the walls harder and the pressure should be higher, but Ar atoms are heavier, which makes up the difference.
choices.rationale: The equality does come from a balance between speed and mass, but the pressure is not higher for He, because the two effects exactly cancel; the statement contradicts the given equal pressures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The He atoms hit the walls more often, but each collision transfers less momentum, so the pressure is the same.
choices.rationale: Correct: same T gives the same average KE; He is lighter and faster, so more collisions per second, each with a smaller momentum change; with equal n, V, T the pressures are equal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Ar atoms are heavier, so they have more kinetic energy and make a higher pressure than He.
choices.rationale: The average kinetic energy depends only on temperature, so Ar atoms do not have more kinetic energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both gases have the same average speed at the same temperature, so the pressures are equal.
choices.rationale: At the same temperature lighter atoms are faster, so the average speeds are not the same.

title: separate collision frequency, momentum per collision and speed in pressure (variant 1)
stem: A rigid container of Ne(g) is heated from 300 K to 600 K. The pressure doubles. Which statement best explains the doubling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The average speed doubles, so the pressure doubles.
choices.rationale: The average speed rises by √2, not by a factor of 2; the pressure doubles because speed enters twice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The atoms strike the walls twice as often, with the same momentum per collision.
choices.rationale: The collision frequency rises by √2 only, and the momentum per collision also rises.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The atoms strike the walls about √2 times as often and with about √2 times the momentum per collision.
choices.rationale: Correct: speed ∝ √T, so doubling T raises the speed by √2; collision frequency ∝ speed and momentum per collision ∝ speed, so pressure ∝ speed² ∝ T, which doubles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The atoms strike the walls at the same rate, but the momentum per collision doubles.
choices.rationale: Faster atoms also reach the walls more often, so the collision rate does not stay the same.

title: separate collision frequency, momentum per collision and speed in pressure (variant 2)
stem: A sample of gas in a cylinder is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature, and the pressure doubles. Which statement best explains the pressure change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The average speed of the molecules doubles because the molecules are closer together.
choices.rationale: Speed depends on temperature, and the temperature is constant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The collisions with the walls become twice as frequent per unit area, while the average speed is unchanged.
choices.rationale: Correct: constant T means the same average KE and speed; half the volume means twice the number density, so twice as many collisions per second per unit wall area.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The average kinetic energy of the molecules doubles because work was done on the gas.
choices.rationale: At constant temperature the work is released as heat to the surroundings and the average kinetic energy stays the same.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The momentum transferred per collision doubles because the molecules are squeezed together.
choices.rationale: Momentum per collision depends on the speed and mass, both unchanged here.

title: separate collision frequency, momentum per collision and speed in pressure (variant 3)
stem: At 400 K, samples of He (4.00 g/mol) and CH₄ (16.0 g/mol) are compared. Which choice gives the correct ratios, He to CH₄, for average speed and for average kinetic energy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Speed ratio 4 : 1; kinetic energy ratio 1 : 1
choices.rationale: The speed ratio is the square root of the molar mass ratio, so 4 comes from leaving out the square root.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Speed ratio 2 : 1; kinetic energy ratio 4 : 1
choices.rationale: The kinetic energy depends on temperature only, so squaring the speed ratio while ignoring the masses is wrong.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Speed ratio 2 : 1; kinetic energy ratio 1 : 1
choices.rationale: Correct: average speed ∝ √(1/M), so the ratio is √(16.0/4.00) = 2; average KE depends only on T, so the ratio is 1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Speed ratio 1 : 1; kinetic energy ratio 1 : 1
choices.rationale: Equal temperature gives equal kinetic energy, not equal speed, because the masses differ.

title: use compressibility data to find real volume and decide attractions vs particle volume
stem: At 300 K and 100 atm, 1.00 mol of CH₄ has Z = PV/(nRT) = 0.87. Use R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) and V = Z·nRT/P. What is the measured volume, and what does the result show?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 0.246 L; CH₄ behaves ideally at this pressure.
choices.rationale: Ideal behavior would give Z = 1.00, and 0.246 L is the ideal volume, not the measured one.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.214 L; attractions between CH₄ molecules pull them closer, so the volume is smaller than the ideal value.
choices.rationale: Correct: ideal V = 1.00 × 0.0821 × 300 / 100 = 0.246 L; real V = 0.87 × 0.246 = 0.214 L; Z < 1 indicates attractions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 0.283 L; the volume of the CH₄ molecules makes the volume larger than the ideal value.
choices.rationale: A volume above ideal would need Z greater than 1, which is the sign of particle volume, but Z is 0.87 here.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0.214 L; the volume of the CH₄ molecules makes the real volume smaller than the ideal value.
choices.rationale: The number is right, but molecular volume would increase the real volume; the smaller volume comes from attractions.

title: use compressibility data to find real volume and decide attractions vs particle volume (variant 1)
stem: At 300 K and 100 atm, 1.00 mol of He has Z = PV/(nRT) = 1.06. Use R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) and V = Z·nRT/P. What is the measured volume, and what does the result show?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 0.246 L; He behaves ideally because it is a noble gas.
choices.rationale: A noble gas still deviates at 100 atm, and Z = 1.06 is not 1.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 0.261 L; the volume of the He atoms themselves becomes significant, so the real volume is larger than the ideal value.
choices.rationale: Correct: ideal V = 0.246 L; real V = 1.06 × 0.246 = 0.261 L; Z > 1 means the finite size of the atoms dominates because He attractions are very weak.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 0.232 L; attractions between He atoms make the volume smaller than the ideal value.
choices.rationale: A smaller volume would need Z < 1, and He has almost no attractions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 0.261 L; attractions between He atoms make the volume larger than the ideal value.
choices.rationale: Attractions pull the molecules together and make the volume smaller, so they cannot explain a larger volume.

title: use compressibility data to find real volume and decide attractions vs particle volume (variant 2)
stem: A 1.00 mol sample of gas in a 0.500 L rigid container at 300 K has a measured pressure of 44 atm. Use R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K). What is the ideal pressure, and what does the comparison show?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 49.3 atm; the measured pressure is lower, which points to attractions between the molecules.
choices.rationale: Correct: P(ideal) = 1.00 × 0.0821 × 300 / 0.500 = 49.3 atm; 44 < 49.3, so attractions reduce the force of collisions with the walls.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 24.6 atm; the measured pressure is higher, which points to the volume of the molecules.
choices.rationale: 24.6 atm forgets to divide by the 0.500 L volume, which then makes the measured value look high.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 49.3 atm; the measured pressure is lower, which points to the volume of the molecules.
choices.rationale: The ideal pressure is right, but molecular volume would raise the pressure above ideal, not lower it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 12.3 atm; the measured pressure is higher, which points to the volume of the molecules.
choices.rationale: 12.3 atm multiplies by the volume instead of dividing by it.

title: use compressibility data to find real volume and decide attractions vs particle volume (variant 3)
stem: A 2.00 mol sample of H₂ in a 1.00 L rigid container at 300 K has a measured pressure of 52.5 atm. Use R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K). What is the ideal pressure, and what does the comparison show?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 24.6 atm; the measured pressure is higher, which points to the volume of the molecules.
choices.rationale: 24.6 atm uses 1.00 mol instead of 2.00 mol.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 49.3 atm; the measured pressure is higher, which points to the volume of the molecules.
choices.rationale: Correct: P(ideal) = 2.00 × 0.0821 × 300 / 1.00 = 49.3 atm; 52.5 > 49.3, so the finite volume of the molecules leaves less free space and raises the pressure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 49.3 atm; the measured pressure is higher, which points to attractions between the molecules.
choices.rationale: Attractions would lower the pressure below the ideal value, not raise it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 98.5 atm; the measured pressure is lower, which points to attractions between the molecules.
choices.rationale: 98.5 atm doubles the amount twice, and the lower-pressure conclusion would not match 52.5 atm anyway.

title: judge which gas sample deviates most from conditions and intermolecular forces
stem: Which sample of gas is expected to deviate most from ideal gas behavior, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ar at 600 K and 1.0 atm, because Ar has the largest atoms of the four samples.
choices.rationale: At 600 K and 1 atm the atoms are fast and far apart, so Ar behaves very nearly ideally.

choices.label: B
choices.text: NH₃ at 250 K and 1.0 atm, because it is only about 10 K above its boiling point (240 K) and its molecules attract each other strongly.
choices.rationale: Correct: deviation is greatest when the gas is close to condensing (low T, strong attractions) or at high pressure; H₂ has very weak attractions and ten atm is modest, while Ar at 600 K and CH₄ at 400 K at 1 atm are hot, low-pressure samples.

choices.label: C
choices.text: H₂ at 300 K and 10 atm, because it is at the highest pressure.
choices.rationale: Ten atm is modest, and H₂ has very weak attractions and tiny molecules, so it stays close to ideal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: CH₄ at 400 K and 1.0 atm, because CH₄ is nonpolar, so its molecules attract strongly.
choices.rationale: Nonpolar molecules have only weak dispersion forces, and at 400 K and 1 atm CH₄ is far above its boiling point.

title: judge which gas sample deviates most from conditions and intermolecular forces (variant 1)
stem: Which sample of gas is expected to deviate most from ideal gas behavior, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ne at 300 K and 20 atm, because 20 atm is the highest pressure listed.
choices.rationale: Ne attractions are extremely weak, and 20 atm at 300 K does not bring the atoms close enough for large deviations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: N₂ at 500 K and 5.0 atm, because it has the largest number of molecules.
choices.rationale: The number of molecules is not a measure of deviation, and N₂ at 500 K is fast and weakly attracting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: SO₂ at 280 K and 1.0 atm, because it is only about 17 K above its boiling point (263 K) and its polar molecules attract each other.
choices.rationale: Correct: SO₂ is a polar gas just above its boiling point, so its attractions are important; Ne, N₂ and He are weakly attracting and the conditions are far from condensation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He at 150 K and 1.0 atm, because it is the coldest sample.
choices.rationale: He has the weakest attractions of any gas, and 150 K is far above its boiling point of 4 K.

title: judge which gas sample deviates most from conditions and intermolecular forces (variant 2)
stem: Carbon dioxide has a critical temperature of 304 K. Under which conditions does CO₂ deviate most from ideal gas behavior, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 500 K and 2.0 atm, because the gas is hot and the molecules are far apart.
choices.rationale: Hot and fairly dilute conditions make CO₂ nearly ideal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 400 K and 1.0 atm, because the pressure is lowest at this temperature.
choices.rationale: Low pressure and high temperature give nearly ideal behavior, since the molecules rarely interact.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 600 K and 0.50 atm, because the molecules are moving fastest.
choices.rationale: Fast molecules at low pressure are the ideal case; fast motion reduces the effect of attractions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 310 K and 50 atm, because the molecules are close together and slow enough for attractions to matter, near the point where CO₂ condenses.
choices.rationale: Correct: deviations grow at high pressure and at temperatures near condensation; 310 K is just above the critical temperature and 50 atm packs the molecules together.

title: judge which gas sample deviates most from conditions and intermolecular forces (variant 3)
stem: Ethane (C₂H₆, 30.1 g/mol) boils at 185 K and nitric oxide (NO, 30.0 g/mol) boils at 121 K. Each gas is at 200 K and 1.0 atm. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: NO deviates more, because its lower boiling point means weaker bonds in the molecule.
choices.rationale: Boiling points reflect forces between molecules, not the strength of the bonds inside them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ethane deviates more, because its higher boiling point shows stronger attractions between molecules, and 200 K is only 15 K above that boiling point.
choices.rationale: Correct: a higher boiling point reflects stronger intermolecular attractions; at 200 K ethane is much closer to condensing than NO.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two gases deviate equally, because their molar masses are almost the same.
choices.rationale: Equal molar mass does not mean equal intermolecular attractions, and the boiling points differ by 64 K.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither gas deviates, because 1.0 atm is a low pressure.
choices.rationale: Low pressure reduces deviation but does not remove it, and ethane at 200 K is close to condensation.

title: ion concentration after mixing two salt solutions
stem: A student mixes 150.0 mL of 0.200 M NaCl(aq) with 100.0 mL of 0.300 M CaCl₂(aq). Assume the volumes are additive and both salts dissociate completely. What is the concentration of Cl⁻ in the mixture?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 0.240 M counts only one Cl⁻ for each formula unit, so the two Cl⁻ in each CaCl₂ are missed.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 0.400 M averages the Cl⁻ concentrations of the two solutions (0.200 and 0.600) without weighting by volume.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 0.600 M is the Cl⁻ concentration of the CaCl₂ solution before mixing, and ignores the NaCl and the dilution.

title: ion concentration after mixing two salt solutions (variant 1)
stem: A student mixes 200.0 mL of 0.150 M Na₂SO₄(aq) with 300.0 mL of 0.100 M NaNO₃(aq). Assume the volumes are additive and both salts dissociate completely. What is the concentration of Na⁺ in the mixture?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 0.120 M counts one Na⁺ per formula unit of Na₂SO₄, so the factor of 2 is missed.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 0.200 M averages the Na⁺ concentrations (0.300 M and 0.100 M) without weighting by volume.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 0.400 M adds the two Na⁺ concentrations and ignores that mixing dilutes both.

title: ion concentration after mixing two salt solutions (variant 2)
stem: A student mixes 100.0 mL of 0.100 M Al(NO₃)₃(aq) with 150.0 mL of 0.200 M KNO₃(aq). Assume the volumes are additive and both salts dissociate completely. What is the concentration of NO₃⁻ in the mixture?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 0.160 M counts one NO₃⁻ per formula unit of Al(NO₃)₃, so the factor of 3 is missed.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 0.250 M averages the NO₃⁻ concentrations (0.300 M and 0.200 M) without weighting by volume.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 0.500 M adds the two NO₃⁻ concentrations and ignores the dilution on mixing.

title: ion concentration after mixing two salt solutions (variant 3)
stem: A student mixes 75.0 mL of 0.200 M MgCl₂(aq) with 125.0 mL of 0.0800 M AlCl₃(aq). Assume the volumes are additive and both salts dissociate completely. What is the concentration of Cl⁻ in the mixture?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 0.125 M counts one Cl⁻ per formula unit, so the subscripts 2 and 3 are missed.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 0.320 M averages the Cl⁻ concentrations (0.400 M and 0.240 M) without weighting by volume.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 0.640 M adds the two Cl⁻ concentrations and ignores the dilution on mixing.

title: two-step serial dilution with final volumes
stem: A stock solution is 0.500 M. A 10.0 mL portion of the stock is diluted with water to a final volume of 100.0 mL (solution 1). Then 20.0 mL of solution 1 is diluted with water to a final volume of 50.0 mL (solution 2). What is the molarity of solution 2?

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 0.0500 M is the concentration of solution 1, and the second dilution was left out.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 0.200 M applies the second dilution to the 0.500 M stock and skips the first dilution.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 0.0143 M treats 50.0 mL as water added, giving 20.0 mL out of 70.0 mL.

title: two-step serial dilution with final volumes (variant 1)
stem: A 1.20 M stock solution is used. A 5.00 mL portion of stock is diluted to a final volume of 250.0 mL (solution 1). Then 10.0 mL of solution 1 is diluted to a final volume of 100.0 mL (solution 2). What is the molarity of solution 2?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 0.0240 M is the concentration of solution 1, and the second dilution was left out.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

stem: A 0.400 M stock solution is used. A 25.0 mL portion of stock is diluted to a final volume of 500.0 mL (solution 1). Then 50.0 mL of solution 1 is diluted to a final volume of 200.0 mL (solution 2). What is the molarity of solution 2?

stem: A 2.00 M stock solution is used. A 1.00 mL portion of stock is diluted to a final volume of 100.0 mL (solution 1). Then 5.00 mL of solution 1 is diluted to a final volume of 250.0 mL (solution 2). What is the molarity of solution 2?

title: what a correct particulate drawing of a dissolved compound must show
stem: A student draws a particulate model of 3 formula units of CaCl₂ dissolved in water. Which description of the drawing is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Three Ca²⁺ ions and six Cl⁻ ions, separated; water molecules around each Ca²⁺ point their O atoms toward the ion and water molecules around each Cl⁻ point their H atoms toward the ion.
choices.rationale: Correct: CaCl₂ is an ionic compound that dissociates into 1 Ca²⁺ and 2 Cl⁻ per unit; the partial negative O of water is attracted to cations and the partial positive H is attracted to anions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Three intact CaCl₂ units, each surrounded by water molecules with the O atoms pointing toward the unit.
choices.rationale: Ionic solids dissociate in water, so the solution has separated ions and not intact units.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Three Ca²⁺ ions and six Cl⁻ ions, separated; water molecules around each Ca²⁺ point their H atoms toward the ion and water molecules around each Cl⁻ point their O atoms toward the ion.
choices.rationale: The orientation is reversed, since the partially negative O atoms are attracted to the positive ions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Three Ca²⁺ ions and three Cl⁻ ions, separated; water molecules around each Ca²⁺ point their O atoms toward the ion and around each Cl⁻ point their H atoms toward the ion.
choices.rationale: Each CaCl₂ unit gives two Cl⁻ ions, so three units must show six Cl⁻ for the charges to balance.

title: what a correct particulate drawing of a dissolved compound must show (variant 1)
stem: A student draws a particulate model of 2 formula units of Al(NO₃)₃ dissolved in water. Which description of the drawing is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Two Al³⁺ ions, six N atoms and eighteen O atoms, all separated, each surrounded by water molecules.
choices.rationale: The covalent bonds inside nitrate are not broken when the salt dissolves, so N and O atoms are not drawn separately.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two Al³⁺ ions and six NO₃⁻ ions, separated and with each NO₃⁻ intact; water O atoms point toward the Al³⁺ ions and water H atoms point toward the NO₃⁻ ions.
choices.rationale: Correct: Al(NO₃)₃ gives 1 Al³⁺ and 3 NO₃⁻ per unit; the polyatomic nitrate ion stays intact in solution; water orients O toward cations and H toward anions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two Al³⁺ ions and two NO₃⁻ ions, separated; water O atoms point toward Al³⁺ and H atoms point toward NO₃⁻.
choices.rationale: Each Al(NO₃)₃ unit supplies three nitrate ions, so two units must show six nitrate ions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two Al³⁺ ions and six NO₃⁻ ions, separated; water H atoms point toward the Al³⁺ ions and water O atoms point toward the NO₃⁻ ions.
choices.rationale: The orientation is reversed, since the partially negative O atoms are attracted to the positive Al³⁺.

title: what a correct particulate drawing of a dissolved compound must show (variant 2)
stem: A student draws a particulate model of 4 formula units of Na₂SO₄ dissolved in water. Which description of the drawing is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eight Na⁺ ions, four S atoms and sixteen O atoms, all separated, each surrounded by water molecules.
choices.rationale: Sulfate is a polyatomic ion whose atoms stay bonded together in solution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four Na⁺ ions and four SO₄²⁻ ions, separated; water O atoms point toward the SO₄²⁻ ions.
choices.rationale: The charges do not balance, since four Na⁺ and four SO₄²⁻ have a net charge of -4, and each unit supplies two Na⁺.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eight Na⁺ ions and four intact SO₄²⁻ ions, separated; water O atoms point toward the Na⁺ ions and water H atoms point toward the SO₄²⁻ ions.
choices.rationale: Correct: Na₂SO₄ gives 2 Na⁺ and 1 SO₄²⁻ per unit, so 4 units give 8 Na⁺ and 4 SO₄²⁻, with sulfate intact; water O toward Na⁺, water H toward SO₄²⁻.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Four intact Na₂SO₄ units, each surrounded by water molecules hydrogen bonded to the O atoms of the sulfate.
choices.rationale: Na₂SO₄ is ionic and dissociates in water, so intact units would not be drawn.

title: what a correct particulate drawing of a dissolved compound must show (variant 3)
stem: A student draws a particulate model of 4 molecules of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, dissolved in water. Glucose is a molecular compound with several O-H groups. Which description of the drawing is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four glucose molecules broken into separate C, H and O atoms spread through the water.
choices.rationale: Dissolving breaks the attractions between molecules and not the covalent bonds inside them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four C₆H₁₁O₆⁻ ions and four H⁺ ions, separated, because glucose has O-H groups.
choices.rationale: Glucose is a molecular compound and a nonelectrolyte, so it does not release H⁺ ions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Four intact glucose molecules, separated from each other, each with water molecules hydrogen bonded to its O-H groups.
choices.rationale: Correct: glucose dissolves as intact molecules because its polar O-H groups form hydrogen bonds with water; it does not form ions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Four glucose molecules clumped into one cluster with water molecules around the outside.
choices.rationale: Dissolved molecules are dispersed individually among the solvent, so a clump would represent undissolved solid.

title: compare solutions from drawings by dividing by volume and counting the right particles
stem: Diagram X represents 100 mL of NaCl(aq) and shows 8 Na⁺ ions and 8 Cl⁻ ions (water not drawn). Diagram Y represents 50 mL of CaCl₂(aq) and shows 3 Ca²⁺ ions and 6 Cl⁻ ions (water not drawn). Which statement correctly compares the solutions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The CaCl₂ solution has the higher concentration of formula units and also the higher concentration of Cl⁻ ions.
choices.rationale: The CaCl₂ solution has more Cl⁻ per mL, but only 0.060 formula units per mL against 0.080 for NaCl.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The NaCl solution has the higher concentration of formula units and also the higher concentration of Cl⁻ ions, because its diagram has more particles.
choices.rationale: Counting particles without dividing by the volume ignores that Y is only 50 mL, so its Cl⁻ concentration is higher.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The NaCl solution has the higher concentration of Cl⁻ ions, because it shows 8 Cl⁻ ions and the CaCl₂ solution shows only 6.
choices.rationale: The number of ions drawn must be divided by the volume represented, and 6 Cl⁻ in 50 mL is more concentrated than 8 Cl⁻ in 100 mL.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The NaCl solution has the higher concentration of formula units, but the CaCl₂ solution has the higher concentration of Cl⁻ ions.
choices.rationale: Correct: formula units per mL: X 8/100 = 0.080, Y 3/50 = 0.060; Cl⁻ per mL: X 8/100 = 0.080, Y 6/50 = 0.120.

title: compare solutions from drawings by dividing by volume and counting the right particles (variant 1)
stem: Diagram X represents 200 mL of NaBr(aq) and shows 12 Na⁺ ions and 12 Br⁻ ions (water not drawn). Diagram Y represents 100 mL of MgBr₂(aq) and shows 5 Mg²⁺ ions and 10 Br⁻ ions (water not drawn). Which statement correctly compares the solutions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The MgBr₂ solution has the higher concentration of formula units and also the higher concentration of Br⁻ ions.
choices.rationale: MgBr₂ has more Br⁻ per mL, but its formula unit concentration (0.050 per mL) is lower than that of NaBr (0.060 per mL).

choices.label: B
choices.text: The NaBr solution has the higher concentration of Br⁻ ions, because its diagram shows more Br⁻ ions.
choices.rationale: The ion count must be divided by the volume, and 10 Br⁻ in 100 mL is more concentrated than 12 Br⁻ in 200 mL.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two solutions have equal concentrations of Br⁻ ions, because each shows the same number of Br⁻ ions per formula unit.
choices.rationale: NaBr gives one Br⁻ per unit and MgBr₂ gives two, so the Br⁻ concentrations are different.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The NaBr solution has the higher concentration of formula units, but the MgBr₂ solution has the higher concentration of Br⁻ ions.

title: compare solutions from drawings by dividing by volume and counting the right particles (variant 2)
stem: Diagram X represents 150 mL of LiCl(aq) and shows 9 Li⁺ ions and 9 Cl⁻ ions (water not drawn). Diagram Y represents 100 mL of AlCl₃(aq) and shows 4 Al³⁺ ions and 12 Cl⁻ ions (water not drawn). Which statement correctly compares the solutions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The AlCl₃ solution has the higher concentration of formula units and also the higher concentration of Cl⁻ ions.
choices.rationale: AlCl₃ has far more Cl⁻ per mL, but only 0.040 formula units per mL against 0.060 for LiCl.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The LiCl solution has the higher concentration of formula units, but the AlCl₃ solution has the higher concentration of Cl⁻ ions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The LiCl solution has the higher concentration of Cl⁻ ions, because its diagram shows 9 Cl⁻ ions in a larger volume.
choices.rationale: The Cl⁻ concentration is the number of ions divided by the volume, and 12 Cl⁻ in 100 mL is double the 9 Cl⁻ in 150 mL.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The LiCl solution is more concentrated in formula units and in Cl⁻ ions, because 18 particles are drawn against 16.
choices.rationale: Totals of 18 and 16 particles ignore the volumes, and AlCl₃ has the higher Cl⁻ concentration.

title: compare solutions from drawings by dividing by volume and counting the right particles (variant 3)
stem: Diagram X represents 100 mL of KCl(aq) and shows 10 K⁺ ions and 10 Cl⁻ ions (water not drawn). Diagram Y represents 50 mL of Na₃PO₄(aq) and shows 3 PO₄³⁻ ions and 9 Na⁺ ions (water not drawn). Which statement correctly compares the solutions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Na₃PO₄ solution has the higher concentration of formula units and also the higher concentration of cations.
choices.rationale: Na₃PO₄ has more cations per mL, but its formula unit concentration (0.060 per mL) is lower than that of KCl (0.100 per mL).

choices.label: B
choices.text: The KCl solution has the higher concentration of cations, because 10 K⁺ ions are drawn against 9 Na⁺ ions.
choices.rationale: The number of ions drawn must be divided by the volume, and 9 Na⁺ in 50 mL is more concentrated than 10 K⁺ in 100 mL.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The KCl solution has the higher concentration of formula units, but the Na₃PO₄ solution has the higher concentration of cations.
choices.rationale: Correct: formula units per mL: X 10/100 = 0.100, Y 3/50 = 0.060; cations per mL: X 10/100 = 0.100, Y 9/50 = 0.180.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two solutions have equal concentrations of cations, because each diagram shows nearly the same number of cations.
choices.rationale: The diagrams show nearly equal cation counts but represent volumes that differ by a factor of two.

title: Rf from origin-line measurements and polarity comparison
stem: A paper chromatography strip uses polar paper and a nonpolar solvent. The starting line was drawn 1.5 cm above the bottom edge. After the run, the center of spot X is 4.5 cm above the bottom edge, the center of spot Y is 6.0 cm above it, and the solvent front is 8.5 cm above it. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Rf of X is 0.53, and X is more polar than Y.
choices.rationale: 0.53 divides the height above the bottom edge instead of the distance from the starting line.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Rf of X is 0.43, and X is more polar than Y.
choices.rationale: Correct: distance moved by X = 4.5 - 1.5 = 3.0 cm; solvent front distance = 8.5 - 1.5 = 7.0 cm; Rf = 3.0/7.0 = 0.43; Y has Rf 4.5/7.0 = 0.64; on polar paper the more polar compound moves less.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Rf of X is 0.43, and X is less polar than Y.
choices.rationale: On a polar stationary phase the compound that moves less is held more strongly, so X is the more polar one.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Rf of X is 0.64, and X is more polar than Y.
choices.rationale: 0.64 is the Rf of spot Y, which was used in place of X.

title: Rf from origin-line measurements and polarity comparison (variant 1)
stem: A thin-layer plate has a nonpolar stationary phase and a polar solvent. The starting line is 2.0 cm above the bottom edge. After the run, spot P is at 5.0 cm, spot Q is at 8.0 cm, and the solvent front is at 10.0 cm above the bottom edge. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Rf of P is 0.38, and P is less polar than Q.
choices.rationale: Correct: Rf(P) = (5.0 - 2.0)/(10.0 - 2.0) = 0.375; Rf(Q) = 0.75; with a nonpolar stationary phase and polar solvent, the more polar compound travels farther, so P (less travel) is less polar.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Rf of P is 0.50, and P is less polar than Q.
choices.rationale: 0.50 divides the height above the bottom edge instead of the distance from the starting line.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Rf of P is 0.38, and P is more polar than Q.
choices.rationale: The rule from polar paper was applied, but with a nonpolar stationary phase the polar compound travels farther.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Rf of P is 0.75, and P is less polar than Q.
choices.rationale: 0.75 is the Rf of spot Q, used in place of P.

title: Rf from origin-line measurements and polarity comparison (variant 2)
stem: A silica (polar) TLC plate is developed with a nonpolar solvent. The starting line is 1.0 cm above the bottom edge and the solvent front is at 7.0 cm. The spots are at 3.0 cm (compound A), 5.5 cm (compound B) and 2.5 cm (compound C). Which choice lists the compounds from least polar to most polar and gives the Rf of A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C, A, B; Rf of A = 0.33
choices.rationale: The order is reversed, since on polar silica the most polar compound (C) moves the least.

choices.label: B
choices.text: B, A, C; Rf of A = 0.43
choices.rationale: Rf = 0.43 divides the spot height above the bottom edge (3.0 cm) by the 7.0 cm front distance, mixing the two measurement bases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: B, A, C; Rf of A = 0.33
choices.rationale: Correct: Rf(A) = (3.0 - 1.0)/(7.0 - 1.0) = 0.33; Rf(B) = 0.75 and Rf(C) = 0.25; on polar silica the compound that travels farthest is least polar, so the order is B, A, C.

choices.label: D
choices.text: C, A, B; Rf of A = 0.43
choices.rationale: Both the order and the distance were wrong, because the most polar compound moves least and the starting line was ignored.

title: Rf from origin-line measurements and polarity comparison (variant 3)
stem: Dye Z is polar. On polar paper the starting line is 1.5 cm above the bottom edge, the dye spot is at 5.0 cm and the solvent front is at 9.0 cm after a run with a mostly nonpolar solvent. A second run uses a more polar solvent mixture. Which choice gives the Rf in the first run and the expected change in the second run?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rf = 0.56; the Rf increases.
choices.rationale: 0.56 divides by the height above the bottom edge rather than the distance from the starting line.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rf = 0.56; the Rf decreases.
choices.rationale: Both the Rf value and the direction are wrong, since the more polar solvent helps the polar dye move.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rf = 0.47; the Rf decreases.
choices.rationale: The Rf is right, but a more polar solvent would not hold a polar dye back; it carries the dye farther.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rf = 0.47; the Rf increases.
choices.rationale: Correct: Rf = (5.0 - 1.5)/(9.0 - 1.5) = 3.5/7.5 = 0.47; a more polar solvent dissolves the polar dye better and competes with the polar paper for it, so the dye moves farther.

title: order of elution or separation sequence from intermolecular forces
stem: A mixture is loaded on a column packed with polar silica, and nonpolar hexane is passed through. Compound 1 is a hydrocarbon, compound 2 is a ketone (C=O, no O-H group) and compound 3 is an alcohol (O-H group, forms hydrogen bonds). Which choice gives the order in which the compounds leave the column and a way to speed up the slowest one?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1, then 2, then 3; adding a more polar solvent such as ethanol to the mobile phase would speed up compound 3.
choices.rationale: Correct: the polar silica holds the most polar compound longest; the hydrocarbon is not retained and elutes first, the ketone next, the alcohol last; a more polar mobile phase competes with the alcohol for the silica.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3, then 2, then 1; adding a more polar solvent such as ethanol would speed up compound 1.
choices.rationale: The order is reversed, since the compound with the strongest attraction to the polar silica (the alcohol) is held longest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1, then 2, then 3; making the mobile phase even less polar would speed up compound 3.
choices.rationale: A less polar solvent competes even less with the polar silica for compound 3, so it would slow compound 3 further.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 2, then 1, then 3; adding a more polar solvent would speed up compound 3.
choices.rationale: The hydrocarbon has no polar groups to bind to silica, so it is not retained any longer than the ketone.

title: order of elution or separation sequence from intermolecular forces (variant 1)
stem: A mixture is separated on a column packed with a nonpolar stationary phase, using a polar mobile phase of water and methanol. Compound P is glucose (very polar), compound Q is benzoic acid (moderately polar) and compound R is a long-chain hydrocarbon (nonpolar). Which choice gives the order in which the compounds leave the column and a way to speed up the slowest one?

choices.label: A
choices.text: R, then Q, then P; making the mobile phase more polar would speed up compound P.
choices.rationale: This is the order for a polar stationary phase, and the polar compound is held longest there, not here.

choices.label: B
choices.text: P, then Q, then R; making the mobile phase more polar would speed up compound R.
choices.rationale: The order is right, but a more polar mobile phase would hold the nonpolar compound back even more.

choices.label: C
choices.text: P, then Q, then R; making the mobile phase less polar (more methanol) would speed up compound R.
choices.rationale: Correct: a nonpolar stationary phase retains nonpolar compounds, so the polar glucose leaves first and the hydrocarbon last; a less polar mobile phase dissolves the hydrocarbon better and carries it along.

choices.label: D
choices.text: R, then Q, then P; making the mobile phase less polar would speed up compound P.
choices.rationale: The order is the reverse of the one expected for a nonpolar stationary phase.

title: order of elution or separation sequence from intermolecular forces (variant 2)
stem: A mixture of pentane (boiling point 36°C), hexane (69°C) and heptane (98°C) is slowly heated in a fractional distillation setup. Which statement correctly gives the first liquid collected and the reason?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heptane, because its larger molecules have stronger dispersion forces and escape the liquid most easily.
choices.rationale: Stronger dispersion forces hold molecules in the liquid, so heptane has the highest boiling point and leaves last.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hexane, because it is the middle component and reaches its boiling point first.
choices.rationale: The order of vaporization follows the boiling points and not the position in the mixture, so hexane comes second.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All three together, because the liquids are miscible and cannot be separated by heating.
choices.rationale: Miscible liquids with different boiling points are exactly what distillation separates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pentane, because its weaker dispersion forces give it the lowest boiling point, so it vaporizes first.
choices.rationale: Correct: smaller nonpolar molecules have weaker dispersion forces and lower boiling points; the lowest-boiling component vaporizes first and is collected first.

title: order of elution or separation sequence from intermolecular forces (variant 3)
stem: A student has a mixture of sand, dissolved NaCl and water. Which procedure recovers the sand, the salt and the water as separate samples?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evaporate the water, then filter the remaining solids to separate the sand from the salt.
choices.rationale: After evaporation the sand and salt are two dry solids, and filtering does not separate them; the water is also lost.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Filter the mixture to remove the sand, then distill the filtrate so that water is collected and the salt remains.
choices.rationale: Correct: sand is insoluble and is removed by filtration; dissolved ions pass through the paper, and distillation separates water from the salt by boiling point.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Distill the mixture, then filter the distillate to remove the salt.
choices.rationale: Distillation gives pure water in the distillate, which contains no salt to filter, and the sand is still in the flask.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Filter the mixture through paper to remove the dissolved NaCl, then boil the filtrate to recover the sand.
choices.rationale: Dissolved ions pass through filter paper, so filtration cannot remove NaCl, and the sand would be caught on the paper instead.

title: crystallized mass from solubility-temperature data scaled by water mass
stem: Approximate solubility of KNO₃ in water: 31 g per 100 g of water at 20°C; 85 g per 100 g at 50°C; 110 g per 100 g at 60°C; 170 g per 100 g at 80°C. A solution saturated at 50°C is made with 200 g of water and is then cooled to 20°C. What mass of KNO₃ crystallizes?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 54 g is the difference per 100 g of water (85 - 31), and it was not doubled for 200 g of water.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 62 g is the mass that stays dissolved at 20°C, not the mass that crystallizes.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 170 g is the total mass that was dissolved at 50°C, and it ignores the KNO₃ that stays in solution at 20°C.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: dissolved at 50°C = 2 × 85 = 170 g; still dissolved at 20°C = 2 × 31 = 62 g; crystallized = 170 - 62 = 108 g.

title: crystallized mass from solubility-temperature data scaled by water mass (variant 1)
stem: Approximate solubility of a salt Q in water: 22 g per 100 g of water at 40°C and 54 g per 100 g at 90°C. A solution saturated at 90°C is made with 150 g of water and is then cooled to 40°C. What mass of salt Q crystallizes?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 32 g is the difference per 100 g of water (54 - 22), and it was not scaled for 150 g of water.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 33 g is the mass that stays dissolved at 40°C, not the mass that crystallizes.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 81 g is the total mass dissolved at 90°C, and it ignores the salt that stays in solution.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: dissolved at 90°C = 1.5 × 54 = 81 g; still dissolved at 40°C = 1.5 × 22 = 33 g; crystallized = 81 - 33 = 48 g.

title: crystallized mass from solubility-temperature data scaled by water mass (variant 2)
stem: Approximate solubility of KNO₃ in water: 31 g per 100 g of water at 20°C; 85 g per 100 g at 50°C; 110 g per 100 g at 60°C; 170 g per 100 g at 80°C. A solution is saturated at 20°C using 300 g of water and is then warmed to 60°C. What additional mass of KNO₃ can dissolve to give a saturated solution at 60°C?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 79 g is the difference per 100 g of water (110 - 31), and it was not scaled for 300 g of water.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: dissolved at 20°C = 3 × 31 = 93 g; capacity at 60°C = 3 × 110 = 330 g; additional = 330 - 93 = 237 g.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 93 g is the mass already dissolved at 20°C, not the additional amount.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 330 g is the total capacity at 60°C, and it ignores the KNO₃ already in solution.

title: crystallized mass from solubility-temperature data scaled by water mass (variant 3)
stem: Approximate solubility of KNO₃ in water: 31 g per 100 g of water at 20°C; 85 g per 100 g at 50°C; 110 g per 100 g at 60°C; 170 g per 100 g at 80°C. A solution saturated at 80°C is made with 50.0 g of water and is then cooled to 20°C. What mass of KNO₃ remains dissolved at 20°C?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Correct: at 20°C, 50.0 g of water holds 0.500 × 31 = 15.5 g (69.5 g of the original 85 g crystallizes).

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 31 g is the solubility per 100 g of water, and it was not scaled to 50.0 g of water.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 69.5 g is the mass that crystallizes, not the mass that remains dissolved.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 85 g is the mass that dissolved in 50.0 g of water at 80°C, before cooling.

title: gas solubility from partial pressure and air composition
stem: The solubility of O₂ in water at 25°C is 1.3 × 10⁻³ M for each 1.0 atm of O₂ partial pressure. Air is 21% O₂ by volume. Water is in equilibrium with air compressed to a total pressure of 3.0 atm. What is the concentration of dissolved O₂?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 3.9 × 10⁻³ M uses the total pressure of 3.0 atm as if all of the gas were O₂.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 2.7 × 10⁻⁴ M is the value for air at 1.0 atm, so the increase to 3.0 atm was ignored.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 2.1 × 10⁻³ M divides the solubility by the partial pressure instead of multiplying.

title: gas solubility from partial pressure and air composition (variant 1)
stem: The solubility of N₂ in water at 25°C is 6.1 × 10⁻⁴ M for each 1.0 atm of N₂ partial pressure. Air is 78% N₂ by volume. Water is in equilibrium with air at a total pressure of 2.0 atm. What is the concentration of dissolved N₂?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 1.2 × 10⁻³ M uses the total pressure of 2.0 atm as if the gas were pure N₂.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 4.8 × 10⁻⁴ M is the value for air at 1.0 atm, so the doubling of the pressure was ignored.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 3.9 × 10⁻⁴ M divides the solubility by the partial pressure instead of multiplying.

title: gas solubility from partial pressure and air composition (variant 2)
stem: The solubility of CO₂ in water at 25°C is 0.034 M for each 1.0 atm of CO₂ partial pressure. A bottle of soda is sealed with CO₂ at 4.0 atm above the liquid. The bottle is opened and left until the liquid has come to equilibrium with the air, where the CO₂ partial pressure is 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ atm. At the same temperature, what is the final concentration of dissolved CO₂?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 0.136 M is the concentration while the bottle was sealed at 4.0 atm, before the gas escaped.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Correct: [CO₂] = 0.034 × 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.4 × 10⁻⁵ M (compared with 0.034 × 4.0 = 0.136 M while sealed).

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 0.034 M is the value for 1.0 atm of CO₂, which is not the CO₂ pressure in air.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 1.4 × 10⁻³ M treats the 0.04% of CO₂ in air as a fraction of 0.04 instead of 0.0004.

title: gas solubility from partial pressure and air composition (variant 3)
stem: The solubility of N₂ in water at 25°C is 6.1 × 10⁻⁴ M for each 1.0 atm of N₂ partial pressure. Air is 78% N₂. At the surface the total pressure is 1.0 atm. A diver breathes air at a total pressure of 4.0 atm, and body water is assumed to come to equilibrium with the N₂ in the air. By how much does the dissolved N₂ concentration increase compared with the surface?

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: 1.9 × 10⁻³ M is the total concentration at depth, and the concentration already present at the surface was not subtracted.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: 4.8 × 10⁻⁴ M is the surface concentration, not the increase.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: 1.8 × 10⁻³ M treats the air as pure N₂ and ignores that only 78% is N₂.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Correct: [N₂] at depth = 6.1 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.78 × 4.0 = 1.9 × 10⁻³ M; at the surface 6.1 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.78 = 4.8 × 10⁻⁴ M; increase = 1.4 × 10⁻³ M.

title: photon energy ratio and region-to-transition matching
stem: A compound absorbs radiation at 3.0 μm (infrared) and at 250 nm (ultraviolet). Which statement correctly compares the two absorptions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 250 nm photons have 12 times the energy of the 3.0 μm photons, and they excite electronic transitions, while the 3.0 μm photons excite bond vibrations.
choices.rationale: Correct: E is proportional to 1/λ, so the energy ratio is 3000 nm / 250 nm = 12; UV photons promote electrons, IR photons change vibrations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 3.0 μm photons have 12 times the energy of the 250 nm photons, and they excite electronic transitions.
choices.rationale: Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, so the longer-wavelength IR photon has the lower energy, not 12 times more.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 250 nm photons have 144 times the energy of the 3.0 μm photons, and they excite electronic transitions.
choices.rationale: The energy ratio is the wavelength ratio itself, not its square.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 250 nm photons have 12 times the energy of the 3.0 μm photons, and they excite bond vibrations.
choices.rationale: The ratio is right, but the UV photons carry enough energy to promote electrons, while bond vibrations need the smaller energy of IR photons.

title: photon energy ratio and region-to-transition matching (variant 1)
stem: A gas absorbs microwave radiation at 3.0 cm and infrared radiation at 3.0 μm. Which statement correctly compares the two absorptions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The microwave photons have 1.0 × 10⁴ times the energy of the IR photons, and they excite molecular vibrations.
choices.rationale: The microwave photon has the longer wavelength, so it has the lower energy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The IR photons have 1.0 × 10⁴ times the energy of the microwave photons; the IR absorption changes the rotations and the microwave absorption changes the vibrations.
choices.rationale: Rotational changes take far less energy than vibrational changes, so the smaller microwave photons match rotations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The IR photons have 1.0 × 10² times the energy of the microwave photons; the IR absorption changes the vibrations and the microwave absorption changes the rotations.
choices.rationale: The energy ratio is the full wavelength ratio of 10⁴, not its square root.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The IR photons have 1.0 × 10⁴ times the energy of the microwave photons; the IR absorption changes the molecular vibrations and the microwave absorption changes the molecular rotations.
choices.rationale: Correct: 3.0 cm / 3.0 μm = 3.0 × 10⁻² m / 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ m = 1.0 × 10⁴; rotational energy changes are smaller than vibrational ones.

title: photon energy ratio and region-to-transition matching (variant 2)
stem: A dye absorbs visible light at 500 nm and infrared radiation at 5.0 μm. Which statement correctly compares the two absorptions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 5.0 μm photons have 10 times the energy of the 500 nm photons, and they excite electronic transitions.
choices.rationale: The longer-wavelength IR photon has the lower energy, not 10 times more.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 500 nm photons have 10 times the energy of the 5.0 μm photons, and they excite electronic transitions, while the 5.0 μm photons excite bond vibrations.
choices.rationale: Correct: 5000 nm / 500 nm = 10; visible photons promote electrons, IR photons change vibrations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 500 nm photons have 100 times the energy of the 5.0 μm photons, and they excite electronic transitions.
choices.rationale: The energy ratio is the wavelength ratio of 10, not its square.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 500 nm photons have 10 times the energy of the 5.0 μm photons, and they excite bond vibrations, while the 5.0 μm photons excite electronic transitions.
choices.rationale: The ratio is right, but the assignments are reversed, since vibrations need less energy than electronic transitions.

title: photon energy ratio and region-to-transition matching (variant 3)
stem: A molecule absorbs ultraviolet radiation at 200 nm and visible light at 600 nm, and both absorptions are caused by electronic transitions. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 200 nm photons have 9.0 times the energy of the 600 nm photons, so the 200 nm absorption involves a larger energy gap.
choices.rationale: The energy ratio equals the wavelength ratio, not its square.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 600 nm photons have 3.0 times the energy of the 200 nm photons, so the 600 nm absorption involves a larger energy gap.
choices.rationale: The shorter wavelength has the higher energy, so the 600 nm photons carry less, not more.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 200 nm photons have 3.0 times the energy of the 600 nm photons, so the 200 nm absorption is a vibrational transition.
choices.rationale: The problem states that both absorptions are electronic, and vibrational transitions need IR photons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 200 nm photons have 3.0 times the energy of the 600 nm photons, so the 200 nm absorption involves a larger energy gap between electronic levels.
choices.rationale: Correct: 600 nm / 200 nm = 3.0; the photon energy matches the gap between electronic energy levels.

title: bond energy per mole versus single-photon energy; intensity misconception
stem: Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ /mol. A C-H bond has a bond energy of 410 kJ/mol. Which light can break a C-H bond by absorption of a single photon per bond?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ultraviolet light at 250 nm, because each photon carries more than 410 kJ per mole of photons.
choices.rationale: Correct: the energy of a mole of photons is 119,600 / λ(nm) kJ/mol: 650 nm gives 184, 450 nm gives 266, 250 nm gives 479, 10 μm gives 12.0; only 250 nm exceeds 410 kJ/mol; the longest wavelength that can break the bond is about 292 nm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A red laser at 650 nm, because red light is the most intense visible light.
choices.rationale: A 650 nm photon carries only about 184 kJ per mole of photons, and color does not make the energy larger.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A blue laser at 450 nm, because blue light carries the most energy of the visible region.
choices.rationale: A 450 nm photon carries about 266 kJ per mole of photons, which is still below 410 kJ/mol.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A very intense infrared source at 10 μm, because it delivers many photons per second.
choices.rationale: Intensity counts photons, but each IR photon at 10 μm carries only about 12 kJ per mole, and photon energies do not add up on one bond.

title: bond energy per mole versus single-photon energy; intensity misconception (variant 1)
stem: Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ /mol. The O-O bond in a peroxide has a bond energy of 142 kJ/mol. Which light can break an O-O bond by absorption of a single photon per bond?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Near-infrared light at 950 nm, because it is close to the energy needed.
choices.rationale: A 950 nm photon carries about 126 kJ per mole of photons, which is below 142 kJ/mol.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infrared light at 1.5 μm, because a strong beam provides many photons.
choices.rationale: Many low-energy photons do not combine on a single bond, and each 1.5 μm photon carries about 80 kJ per mole.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Near-infrared light at 780 nm, because each photon carries more than 142 kJ per mole of photons.
choices.rationale: Correct: 780 nm photons carry 153 kJ per mole of photons, above 142 kJ/mol; the threshold is about 843 nm; 950 nm gives 126, 1.5 μm gives 80, 20 μm gives 6.0.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Far-infrared light at 20 μm, because infrared radiation is absorbed by bond vibrations.
choices.rationale: Absorption by vibrations does not break the bond, since each 20 μm photon carries only about 6 kJ per mole.

title: bond energy per mole versus single-photon energy; intensity misconception (variant 2)
stem: Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ /mol. The N≡N bond in N₂ has a bond energy of 945 kJ/mol. Which light can break an N≡N bond by absorption of a single photon per bond?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blue light at 450 nm, because it is the highest-energy visible light.
choices.rationale: A 450 nm photon carries about 266 kJ per mole of photons, far below 945 kJ/mol.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ultraviolet light at 250 nm, because ultraviolet light breaks bonds.
choices.rationale: A 250 nm photon carries about 479 kJ per mole of photons, which can break a weaker bond but not this triple bond.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ultraviolet light at 150 nm, because it is far into the ultraviolet.
choices.rationale: A 150 nm photon carries about 797 kJ per mole of photons, still below 945 kJ/mol.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Far-ultraviolet light at 100 nm, because each photon carries more than 945 kJ per mole of photons.
choices.rationale: Correct: photon energy per mole = 119,600 / λ(nm): 450 nm gives 266, 250 nm gives 479, 150 nm gives 797, 100 nm gives 1196 kJ/mol; the threshold is about 127 nm.

title: bond energy per mole versus single-photon energy; intensity misconception (variant 3)
stem: Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s and Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ /mol. The Cl-Cl bond in Cl₂ has a bond energy of 242 kJ/mol. Which light can break a Cl-Cl bond by absorption of a single photon per bond?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Red light at 700 nm, because red light is the lowest-energy visible light and so is gentlest.
choices.rationale: A 700 nm photon carries only about 171 kJ per mole of photons, below 242 kJ/mol.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Green light at 550 nm, because green is in the middle of the visible region.
choices.rationale: A 550 nm photon carries about 218 kJ per mole of photons, just below 242 kJ/mol.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blue light at 450 nm, because each photon carries more than 242 kJ per mole of photons.
choices.rationale: Correct: photon energy per mole = 119,600 / λ(nm): 700 nm gives 171, 550 nm gives 218, 450 nm gives 266, 10 μm gives 12.0 kJ/mol; the threshold is about 494 nm.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An intense infrared lamp at 10 μm, because it can deliver the most photons.
choices.rationale: Intensity does not matter, because each 10 μm photon carries only about 12 kJ per mole of photons.

title: separate frequency effects (KE, threshold) from intensity effects
stem: A metal has a threshold frequency of 5.0 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹. Three lights shine on it: light X has frequency 7.0 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹ and low intensity; light Y has frequency 6.0 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹ and 10 times the intensity of X; light Z has frequency 4.0 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹ and 1000 times the intensity of X. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Light Z ejects electrons with the largest kinetic energy, because its intensity is the greatest.
choices.rationale: Z is below the threshold frequency, so its photons cannot eject any electron regardless of intensity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Light Y ejects electrons with the largest kinetic energy, because it is 10 times as intense as X.
choices.rationale: Intensity changes how many electrons are ejected, but the maximum kinetic energy depends only on the frequency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Light X gives the electrons with the greatest maximum kinetic energy; light Y gives electrons with less, even though it is more intense; light Z ejects no electrons.
choices.rationale: Correct: maximum KE = hν - Φ rises with frequency only; Z is below the threshold, so no photon has enough energy no matter how many arrive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All three lights eject electrons, because enough intensity can make up for a low frequency.
choices.rationale: An electron absorbs one photon at a time, so many low-energy photons cannot combine to eject it.

title: separate frequency effects (KE, threshold) from intensity effects (variant 1)
stem: A metal has a threshold wavelength of 500 nm. Light P has a wavelength of 400 nm and a low intensity. Light Q has a wavelength of 450 nm and 20 times the intensity of P. Light R has a wavelength of 550 nm and 500 times the intensity of P. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Light P gives the electrons with the greatest maximum kinetic energy; light Q gives electrons with less, even though it is more intense; light R ejects no electrons.
choices.rationale: Correct: ν = c/λ, so P is 7.5 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹, Q is 6.7 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹ and R is 5.5 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹, against a threshold of 6.0 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹; R is below the threshold.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Light R ejects electrons with the largest kinetic energy, because its intensity is the greatest.
choices.rationale: R has a wavelength longer than the threshold wavelength, so its photons cannot eject electrons.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Light Q ejects electrons with the largest kinetic energy, because both P and Q are above the threshold and Q is more intense.
choices.rationale: Intensity raises the number of electrons and not their maximum kinetic energy, and P has the higher frequency.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All three lights eject electrons, but those from light R have the smallest kinetic energy.
choices.rationale: Light R is below the threshold frequency, so it ejects none.

title: separate frequency effects (KE, threshold) from intensity effects (variant 2)
stem: Light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹ ejects electrons from a metal with a threshold frequency of 5.0 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹. Which change would double the number of electrons ejected per second without changing their maximum kinetic energy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Double the frequency of the light at the same intensity.
choices.rationale: Doubling the frequency raises the maximum kinetic energy, so that condition is not met.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Switch to a metal with a lower threshold frequency.
choices.rationale: A lower threshold frequency lowers the work function, which raises the maximum kinetic energy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Double the intensity of the light at the same frequency.
choices.rationale: Correct: the electron count follows the number of photons, which rises with intensity; the maximum KE depends only on frequency and the metal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Halve the frequency of the light and double its intensity.
choices.rationale: Halving the frequency to 4.0 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹ goes below the threshold, so no electrons are ejected at all.

title: separate frequency effects (KE, threshold) from intensity effects (variant 3)
stem: Two metals are lit with 450 nm light (photon energy 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). Metal 1 has a work function of 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and metal 2 has a work function of 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both metals emit electrons, and the electrons from metal 1 have the higher maximum kinetic energy.
choices.rationale: The photon energy is below the work function of metal 2, so metal 2 emits no electrons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Metal 1 emits electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of about 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and metal 2 emits none.
choices.rationale: The maximum kinetic energy is the photon energy minus the work function, not the photon energy itself.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metal 1 emits electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of about 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and metal 2 emits none whatever the intensity.
choices.rationale: Correct: photon energy = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸ / 450 × 10⁻⁹ = 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; metal 1: KE = 4.4 - 3.0 = 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; metal 2: 4.4 < 4.5, so the photons are below its threshold.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Metal 1 emits electrons with a maximum kinetic energy of about 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, and metal 2 also emits at high intensity, with lower kinetic energy.
choices.rationale: Electrons absorb one photon at a time, so a high intensity cannot make up for photons that are too low in energy.

title: threshold wavelength from photon energy and KE
stem: Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Light of wavelength 400 nm ejects electrons from a metal with a maximum kinetic energy of 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the threshold wavelength of the metal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 573 nm
choices.rationale: Correct: E(photon) = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; Φ = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ - 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 3.47 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; λ₀ = hc/Φ = 573 nm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 307 nm
choices.rationale: 307 nm adds the kinetic energy to the photon energy instead of subtracting it to find the work function.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 400 nm
choices.rationale: 400 nm treats the photon energy as the work function, which would leave no kinetic energy.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: 1330 nm converts the kinetic energy itself into a wavelength, and the kinetic energy is not the work function.

title: threshold wavelength from photon energy and KE (variant 1)
stem: Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Light of wavelength 300 nm ejects electrons from a metal with a maximum kinetic energy of 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the threshold wavelength of the metal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 230 nm
choices.rationale: 230 nm adds the kinetic energy to the photon energy instead of subtracting it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 430 nm
choices.rationale: Correct: E(photon) = 6.63 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; Φ = 6.63 × 10⁻¹⁹ - 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.63 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; λ₀ = hc/Φ = 430 nm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 300 nm
choices.rationale: 300 nm treats the photon energy as the work function, which would leave no kinetic energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 994 nm

stem: Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Light of wavelength 250 nm ejects electrons from a metal with a maximum kinetic energy of 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the threshold wavelength of the metal?

title: threshold wavelength from photon energy and KE (variant 3)
stem: Use h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Light of wavelength 500 nm ejects electrons from a metal with a maximum kinetic energy of 8.0 × 10⁻²⁰ J. What is the threshold wavelength of the metal?
